{{Johan Cruyff series}}
'''Hendrik Johannes Cruijff''' (25 April 1947 – 24 March 2016), internationally known as '''Johan Cruyff'''{{efn-ua|Commonly known in Dutch as '''Johan Cruijff'''}}{{efn-ua|{{IPA|nl|ˈjoːɦɑŋ ˈkrœyf|lang|JohanCruiff.ogg}}}} was a Dutch professional [[Association football|football]] player and [[Manager (association football)|manager]]. Regarded as one of the greatest players in history and as the greatest Dutch footballer ever, he won the [[Ballon d'Or]] three times, in [[1971 Ballon d'Or|1971]], [[1973 Ballon d'Or|1973]], and [[1974 Ballon d'Or|1974]]. Cruyff was a proponent of the football philosophy known as [[Total Football]], developed by [[Rinus Michels]], both as a player and a manager. Because of the far-reaching impact of his playing style and his coaching ideas, he is widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in modern football, and he is also regarded as one of the greatest managers of all time.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-08-09 |title=Johan Cruyff: The Creator of the Barcelona Dream Team's All-Time Best XI |url=https://www.si.com/soccer/2019/08/09/johan-cruyff-creator-barcelona-dream-teams-all-time-best-xi |access-date=2026-07-23 |website=SI |language=en-US}}</ref>

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, [[Football in the Netherlands|Dutch football]] rose from a semi-professional and obscure level to become a powerhouse in the sport. The Netherlands qualified for the [[1974 FIFA World Cup]], their [[Netherlands at the FIFA World Cup|first appearance in the competition in 36 years]]. With three goals and three assists, Cruyff led the [[Netherlands national football team|Netherlands]] to the final, where they lost to [[Germany national football team|West Germany]]; nonetheless, he received the [[Golden Ball (FIFA)|Golden Ball]] as player of the tournament. After finishing third in [[UEFA Euro 1976]], Cruyff refused to play in the [[1978 FIFA World Cup]] after a kidnapping attempt targeting him and his family in their [[Barcelona]] home led to his retirement from international football.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Doyle |first=Paul |date=2008-04-16 |title=Kidnappers made Cruyff miss World Cup |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/apr/16/newsstory.sport15 |access-date=2026-07-23 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

At club level, Cruyff started his career at [[AFC Ajax|Ajax]] in 1964, where he won six [[Eredivisie]] titles, three [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]]s, and one [[1972 Intercontinental Cup|Intercontinental Cup]]. He moved to [[FC Barcelona]] in 1973, winning the [[La Liga]] title in [[1973–74 La Liga|1973–74]], the club's first in 14 years, and the [[Copa del Rey]] once. After stints at the [[Los Angeles Aztecs]] and the [[Washington Diplomats]] in the United States and at [[Levante UD|Levante]] in Spain, Cruyff returned to Ajax in 1981, winning two further Eredivisie titles. As the club refused to extend his contract, Cruyff moved to main rivals [[Feyenoord]] in 1983, where he won the [[Double (association football)|double]] (Eredivisie and [[KNVB Cup]]) in his first and only season at the club. After retiring from playing in 1984, Cruyff became a highly successful manager of Ajax and Barcelona, winning the [[1987 European Cup Winners' Cup final|1987 European Cup Winners' Cup]] at Ajax, and four La Liga titles and one European Cup at Barcelona. After his dismissal in 1996, he remained an advisor to both Ajax and Barcelona. His son [[Jordi Cruyff|Jordi]] also played football professionally for Barcelona.

Cruyff founded the [[Johan Cruyff Foundation]] in 1997, which is intended to help disadvantaged children and those with special educational needs. In addition, he is the originator of several catchphrases and aphorisms, known as ''[[Cruijffiaans]]'', that have entered everyday language, especially in the Netherlands and to some extent in Spain. In 1999, Cruyff was voted European Player of the Century in an election held by the [[International Federation of Football History & Statistics]], and came second behind [[Pelé]] in their [[FIFA Player of the Century#Vote specialists (IFFHS)|World Player of the Century]] poll.

==Early life==
Hendrik Johannes "Johan" Cruyff was born on 25 April 1947 in the [[:nl:Burgerziekenhuis|Burgerziekenhuis]] in [[Amsterdam]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Johan Cruyff |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Johan-Cruyff |access-date=4 September 2023 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en |archive-date=4 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220804131620/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Johan-Cruyff |url-status=live }}</ref> He grew up on a street five minutes away from [[AFC Ajax|Ajax]]'s stadium, his first football club. Johan was the second son of Hermanus Cornelis Cruijff (1913–1959) and Petronella Bernarda Draaijer (1917–2007), from a humble, working-class background in east Amsterdam. Cruyff grew up at [[:nl:Akkerstraat|Akkerstraat]] 32 in the [[Betondorp]] ('concrete village') neighbourhood,{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=9}} a district whose architectural style was described as "[[brutalist]]".{{sfn|Bollen|2021|page=20}} Akkerstraat was five minutes away from [[De Meer Stadion]], where the football club Ajax Amsterdam played its home games. His father Manus was a fan of Ajax. The environment in which the Cruyffs grew up is described by his biographer Auke Kok as business- and market-oriented, which distanced itself from leftist ideas.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=10}} The young Cruyff was shaped by [[Calvinism]]; while he was considered a devout person and often referred to God, he later also experimented with spiritualistic practices to make contact with his deceased father.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=385}}

At school, Cruyff at most showed inconsistent performance and had twice to repeat a school year. Looking back on his youth, Cruyff later expressed the suspicion that his mixed academic performance and his persistent restlessness were due to [[Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder|ADHD]].{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=13}} He had a close relationship with his older brother Henny, who was two and a half years his senior,{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=10}} during his youth. Observers originally considered Henny more talented than Johan, but he did not make the leap to the professional team. The regretful Cruyff saw the reason for this in Henny's lack of focus on football; unlike himself, Henny had never regarded football as the top priority in his life. Henny later opened a sports shop and sought to capitalise on the family connection, among other things, by arranging trips to Barcelona that, as a promotional promise, also offered tours of Cruyff's estate. His attempts to manage Cruyff were blocked by Johan's father-in-law, [[:nl:Cor Coster|Cor Coster]]. The two brothers then fell out permanently in the 1980s, and Henny published a book in which he accused Coster of having been a member of the [[Waffen-SS]] during the [[German occupation of the Netherlands|German occupation of the Netherlands in the Second World War]]. The allegation was not supported by research.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=476}}

Already in his first years as a professional footballer, Cruyff anglicised his last name; while in his native Netherlands he continues to be known as Cruijff, the anglicised version of his last name has become established in the rest of the world.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=80}}

On 8 July 1959, Cruyff's father died from a heart attack.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=19}} His mother Nel could not continue running the vegetable shop alone and had to give up the business. Instead, she was forced to work as a cleaner at Ajax Amsterdam, cleaning the lockers there.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=62}} There she met Henk Angel (the caretaker at Ajax), with whom she entered into a second marriage. For Cruyff, the death of his father was both a tragedy and a formative event; throughout his life, he was always haunted by the fear of dying at a young age himself. Additionally, the sudden death of his father and the resulting economic consequences for the family became a driving force for him to accumulate as much money as possible in as short a time as possible in order to support and provide security for his biological and stepfamily.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=62}}

Throughout his life, Cruyff remained in the judgment of his biographers a typical "Amsterdammer" with all the character traits that are, partly stereotypically, attributed to the people of Amsterdam. In this way, he displayed the typical arrogance of a big city resident attributed to Amsterdammers by the rest of the Netherlands.{{sfn|Wilson|2018|page=42}} He was also characterised as a classic know-it-all; countless anecdotes circulate about Cruyff trying to instruct others at every opportunity.{{sfn|van den Boogaard|2021|page=106}} In addition, the fast-talking, talkative Cruyff had an unrestrained urge to communicate and enjoyed discussing passionately; even as World Footballer, he gave long interviews to school magazines. Furthermore, he remained loyal to the working-class dialect of his Amsterdam neighbourhood;{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=467}} as a new younger generation pushed into public life in the Netherlands from the 1980s onwards due to rising educational levels, there were initially numerous parodists in the Netherlands (and later also in Spain), who imitated Cruyff's [[idiosyncratic]] language.

==Club career==
===''Gloria Ajax'' and the golden era of Total Football===
{{See also|History of AFC Ajax#Gloria Ajax: European dominance and treble|l1=Gloria Ajax (AFC Ajax)|Total Football|l2=Total Football (Totaalvoetbal)}}
[[File:Johan Cruijff (1965).jpg|thumb|upright|left|Cruyff in October 1965]]

Cruyff joined the Ajax youth system on his tenth birthday. Cruyff and his friends would frequently visit a "playground" in their neighborhood and Ajax youth coach Jany van der Veen, who lived close by, noticed Cruyff's talent and decided to offer him a place at Ajax without a formal trial.<ref name="Early life">{{cite web |url=http://www.benefoot.net/johan-cruijff-a-mortal-with-the-potential-of-a-superman/ |author=Ramesh, Priya |title=''Johan Cruijff: A mortal with the potential of a superman'' |publisher=Benefoot.net |date=1 April 2016 |access-date=9 April 2016 |archive-date=28 December 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171228171718/http://www.benefoot.net/johan-cruijff-a-mortal-with-the-potential-of-a-superman/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Cruyff suffered from physical underdevelopment when he joined the Ajax academy and head coach [[Vic Buckingham]] urged him to go to the gym while providing him with better nutrition.<ref name="hpdetijd.nl">{{cite web | title=Profiel: De jonge jaren van Johan Cruijff | date=24 March 2016 | url=https://www.hpdetijd.nl/nieuws/sport/38072/profiel-de-jonge-jaren-van-johan-cruijff }}</ref> When he first joined Ajax, Cruyff preferred [[baseball in the Netherlands|baseball]] and continued to play the sport until age fifteen when he quit at the urging of his coaches.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Stevens |first1=Samuel |title=14 things you didn't know about Dutch legend Cruyff |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/news/johan-cruyff-dead-14-things-you-didn-t-know-about-the-dutch-legend-a6950186.html |access-date=3 June 2022 |work=[[The Independent]] |date=24 March 2016 |language=en |archive-date=30 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230730142930/https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/news/johan-cruyff-dead-14-things-you-didn-t-know-about-the-dutch-legend-a6950186.html |url-status=live }}</ref> At that age, Cruyff quit his secondary education without a [[diploma]] after staying down twice.<ref name="hpdetijd.nl"/>

Cruyff made his first team debut on 15 November 1964 for Ajax Amsterdam in a 1–3 defeat against GVAV Groningen (since 1971 FC Groningen).{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=29}} In his second match, his home debut against [[PSV Eindhoven]], he scored a goal.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=29}} The following match against Feyenoord Rotterdam was lost 9–4, and after a draw the following week, Ajax were close to relegation. The management lost faith in Vic Buckingham and forced his dismissal on 21 January 1965.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=30}}

[[File:Johan Cruijff opent een drankenwinkel op Beukenplein Amsterdam. Cruijff geeft ha, Bestanddeelnr 922-9725.jpg|thumb|upright|Cruyff signs autographs in Amsterdam (1969)]]
The 36-year-old [[Rinus Michels]] was hired as the new coach. Michels, a sports teacher for deaf children, had previously played for Ajax himself. His job description as coach included team training three evenings a week. However, the ambitious Michels soon began taking radical steps to professionalise the club.{{sfn|Schulze-Marmeling|2012|page=77}} Michels placed great emphasis on iron discipline and was soon nicknamed ''De Generaal'' ('The General') by his players.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=34}} He introduced training camps and had the players complete three training sessions a day, as well as a practice match in the evening. Cruyff, in particular, who had become a chain smoker in his youth, hated the rigid training and occasionally tried to hide during runs in the woods. Michels quickly took further steps toward professionalisation. Many players were part-time or amateur players who had another (main) job.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=93}} Cruyff had been a sort of 'jack-of-all-trades' at a printing company.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=37}}

Michels prohibited any secondary activities and turned the players into professional footballers. This was financed by a number of sponsors, including collaborators who had done business with the German occupiers [[Netherlands in World War II|during the war]] and wanted to clear their names, as well as Jewish businessmen, who had survived the war and saw Ajax as a surrogate family.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=64}}{{sfn|Bollen|2021|page=24}} The image of Ajax as a club with a certain Jewish flair had long been established and in the following years was repeatedly emphasised by the player generation around Cruyff (more in a symbolic and playful manner).{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=299}} This ahistorical stylisation began to develop a dynamic of its own especially from the 1980s onwards, when even the fans of the club Ajax stylised it as the 'Jewish club' and, in response, fans of the arch-rival Feyenoord Rotterdam began to sing [[Antisemitism|antisemitic]] chants and make references to the Holocaust in performances. Originally seen as a symbol of football tribalism,{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=301}} this sparked a societal debate in the Netherlands in the early 2000s.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=302}}

[[File:Benfica tegen Ajax 1-3 elftal Benfica, Bestanddeelnr 922-1225.jpg|thumb|Rinus Michels and Cruyff]]
Tactically, Michels adapted to the opponent and flexibly switched between a 5-3-2 and a 4-2-4 formation. In the 1969–1970 season, he permanently switched to a 4–3–3.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=58}} Michels placed great emphasis on aggressive tackling and physical dominance to stifle the opponent.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=222}} His team also used [[Pressing (association football tactic)|Pressing]] – internally referred to as "hunting" – which was intended to put pressure on the opponent in possession of the ball.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=61}} What was new was the concept of space on the pitch, which Ajax conceived in an abstract and distinctive way. British author [[David Winner (writer)|David Winner]] emphasises that this was unique and concludes that this concept could only have arisen in the Netherlands with its very different understanding of the environment and nature.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=71}} Cruyff and his teammates maximised the playing area when in possession by shifting the play to the wings. Conversely, when losing possession, they minimised the space by pushing their defensive line up close to the halfway line, pressing into the opponent's half, or playing the offside trap to further narrow the space.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=71}} Ajax was also characterised by constant positional changes. Michels claimed the innovation of these constant positional changes for himself; as Ajax regularly dominated their opponents in the Eredivisie in the late 1960s, they increasingly encountered densely packed defensive lines. To address this problem, he wanted to integrate midfielders and defenders into the attack, which resulted in the positional changes.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=59}}

The extent of Cruyff's contribution to these innovations is disputed.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=65}} While Michels' contribution as coach is undisputed, the contributions of the players as a whole, and Cruyff himself, are equally emphasised. Ajax's group of players was considered the embodiment of the individualistic post-war [[Baby Boomer Generation]], who did not readily accept authority and strove for self-realisation.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=72}} Discussions among themselves about hierarchies within the team and tactics were practically a daily occurrence. The high defensive line, in its later form, was also partly initiated by the players, who wanted to conserve energy by playing on a smaller field. Cruyff, in turn, was the dominant, outstanding player who clearly stood out from this group of talented players. Cruyff, as a centre forward, already practiced what subsequently became known as the false nine, dropping back to the wings or deep into midfield to either create an overload there (if his direct opponent held his position) or to open up the space freed up in his position (if his opponent followed him) for his teammates.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=68}} As the linchpin of this model, Cruyff was only nominally positioned as a centre forward, simultaneously acting as playmaker, goalscorer, and crosser. His penchant for this constant shifting of positions is also considered by the British author [[Simon Kuper]] to be the very reason for Ajax's trademark of constant positional changes (Cruyff called it "controlled chaos"),{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=66}} as his teammates adjusted to him and adapted intuitively.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=67}} Undoubtedly, as Cruyff grew older and began discussing tactics more frequently with his teammates, his influence within the team steadily increased. As the finisher on the pitch, Cruyff assumed the role of a player-coach during these years, appearing almost everywhere on the field, constantly coaching his teammates, giving them instructions, and ordering changes in formation and position whenever he deemed it necessary. He sometimes even demanded substitutions from the bench. Looking back, [[Arsène Wenger]] emphasised that it was practically impossible to copy Ajax because the figure of the coaching player Cruyff was unique.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=69}}

[[File:Ajax tegen ADO 2-1. Cruijff omspeelt drie ADO-verdedigers, Bestanddeelnr 921-3886.jpg|thumb|upright|Cruyff dribbles past three defenders from Den Haag, 26 May 1968.]]
Cruyff's relationship with Michels had features of a father-son relationship. Simon Kuper compared it to the [[Lennon–McCartney]] partnership.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=65}} As a creative partnership, they were a mutual inspiration and benefited from each other; moreover, they were clearly the driving forces of the club. On the other hand, they rubbed each other the wrong way, and the relationship also showed clear elements of competition. Michels and Cruyff both strove for dominance within the team. Cruyff repeatedly changed Michels' instructions on the field on his own initiative and often deliberately undermined the coach's directions, which led to outbursts of anger from Michels and loud arguments between the two.{{sfn|van den Boogaard|2021|page=112}} Michels also suspected the somewhat hypochondriacal Cruyff of feigning injuries.{{sfn|van den Boogaard|2021|page=97}} Cruyff adopted from Michels the conflict model that Michels had implemented to create creative friction, and which became part of his own credo{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=62}} – but, as Kuper argues, this was actually just a pretext for Cruyff's combative personality. With "[[Total Football]]" (as the Ajax style was dubbed in 1965), Ajax initially became the dominant force in Dutch football, winning the league title in 1966, 1967, 1968, and 1970.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=56}}

In the early 1970s, Ajax shifted the balance of power in international football. During the 1960s, the football world had been dominated by the Italian [[Catenaccio]], a style based purely on defense. Its leading exponents, [[AC Milan]] and [[Inter Milan]], had each won the European Cup (predecessor to the Champions League) and the [[Intercontinental Cup (1960–2004)|Intercontinental Cup]] twice.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=66}} Ajax's victory over Inter Milan in the 1972 European Cup final, a classic clash of systems, was portrayed in many newspapers as the end of Catenaccio. Football writer and novelist [[Brian Glanville]] saw Catenaccio completely overshadowed by Total Football.<ref>Brian Glanville: ''Champions of Europe.'' Guiness, London 1991, p. 126, quoted in John Foot: ''Calcio. A History of Italian Football.'' Harper Collins, London 2006, p. 229.</ref> The Ajax example first caught on in the Eredivisie in the 1970s, where other clubs like Feyenoord also adopted elements of Total Football and incorporated more frequent positional changes into their game. Subsequently, other clubs, for example in England, also tried to adopt elements of the Ajax style, but with far less success.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=73}}

[[File:Europacup I. Ajax tegen Liverpool 5-1, Johan Cruijff in duel, Bestanddeelnr 919-8589.jpg|thumb|right|Cruyff playing for Ajax taking on [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] defender [[Tommy Smith (footballer, born 1945)|Tommy Smith]] in a European Cup game in December 1966]]
In his early years, Cruyff's performances were inconsistent; at times his enormous talent shone through, while at other times he disappeared in big games and failed to make any significant impact on the game.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=65}} Furthermore, he was frequently injured or complained of minor ailments.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=70}} Michels suspected Cruyff more than once of feigning injuries.{{sfn|van den Boogaard|2021|page=61}} Due to his early tendendency to avoid passing the ball, instead repeatedly getting lost in dribbling and solo runs, he was unpopular with his teammates on the pitch. His position varied in his early years; when he was not yet a regular starter, he was used not only as a centre-forward but also as a substitute on the wing or in midfield.

Cruyff really started to make an impression in the 1965–66 season and established himself as a regular first team player after scoring two goals against [[AFC DWS|DWS]] in the Olympic stadium on 24 October 1965 in a 2–0 victory. In the seven games that winter, he scored eight times and in March 1966 scored the first three goals in a league game against Telstar in a 6–2 win. Four days later, in a cup game against [[BV Veendam|Veendam]] in a 7–0 win, he scored four goals. In total that season, Cruyff scored 25 goals in 23 games, and Ajax won the league championship.<ref name="FIFA_Profile">{{cite web |title=The Netherlands' Grand Master |url=http://www.fifa.com/fifa-tournaments/players-coaches/people=1043/profile.html |website=FIFA.com |access-date=2014-05-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150930160041/http://www.fifa.com/fifa-tournaments/players-coaches/people=1043/profile.html |archive-date=2015-09-30 |url-status=dead |language=en}}</ref>

[[File:Feyenoord tegen Ajax 1-0. Nummer 26 Israel in duel met Cruyff.jpg|thumb|right|Cruyff was instrumental in Ajax's dominance of [[European football]] in the early 1970s. He played for Ajax from 1957 to 1973 and 1981 to 1983 (seen here in 1967 against Feyenoord).]]
The [[1966–67 Eredivisie|1966–67 season]] was another big step for Cruyff; he was already a regular starter at the beginning of the season; he displaced the experienced [[Henk Groot]] from the forward line, who moved into midfield and formed the dominant trio in the team with Cruyff and [[Piet Keizer]].{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=68}} Ajax won the championship title and regularly outclassed their opponents with a flurry of goals – at the end of the season they had a record of 122 goals.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=94}} Cruyff ended the season as the leading goalscorer in the [[Eredivisie]] with 33. Ajax also won the [[KNVB Cup]], for Cruyff's first "double".<ref name="FIFA_Profile"/> Internationally, Ajax faced [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] in a pivotal match – Winner calls it the breakthrough that marked Ajax's first success on the international stage – on 7 December 1966, in Amsterdam. Ajax dominated and won 5–1.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=41}} In the return leg in Liverpool, Cruyff scored two goals to secure a 2–2 draw.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=42}} The next round against Dukla Prague brought disappointment, and Ajax were eliminated.

Ajax won the league for the third successive year in the [[1967–68 Eredivisie|1967–68 season]]. Cruyff was also named Dutch footballer of the year for the second successive time, a feat he repeated in 1969.<ref name="FIFA_Profile"/> In the European Cup, Ajax were eliminated by [[Real Madrid CF|Real Madrid]] after extra time; in Madrid, Ajax missed numerous clear-cut chances, Cruyff himself stood in front of the goalkeeper shortly before the end of the game and, after a brief hesitation, missed.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=100}} The following season, the team's focus shifted even more towards the European Cup;{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=122}} for the first time in years, Ajax finished second in the Eredivisie. In the second round, Ajax beat Istanbul in a famous match played on a mud pitch, with Cruyff scoring the winning goal; the game became known in the Netherlands as the "Hell of Fenerbahce".{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=192}} In the quarter-finals against Benfica Lisbon, Ajax overcame a 1–3 deficit from the first leg, necessitating a replay; Ajax won this 3–0 in neutral Paris. In the semi-finals, they defeated Sparta Trnava.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=56}} The final brought disappointment; Milan's packed defense and Giovanni Trapattoni's consistent man-marking of Cruyff resulted in a one-sided 4–1 victory. Cruyff subsequently faced heavy criticism from coach Michels and the press.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=146}}

[[File:Ajax tegen FC Utrecht 7-1; Johan Cruyff maakt derde doelpunt.jpg|thumb|Cruyff scores the third goal in a 7–1 win against [[FC Utrecht]] (13 December 1970)]]
The following season, a rejuvenated Ajax team won the championship convincingly. at the beginning of the [[1970–71 Eredivisie|1970–71 season]], he suffered a groin injury. He made his comeback on 30 October 1970 against [[PSV Eindhoven|PSV]], and rather than wear his usual number 9, which was in use by [[Gerrie Mühren]], he instead used number 14.<ref name="FIFA_Profile"/> From then on, he only wore number 14 for Ajax. Although it was very uncommon in those days for the starters of a game not to play with numbers 1 to 11, from that moment onwards, Cruyff wore number 14, even with the [[Netherlands national football team|Dutch national team]]. There was a documentary on Cruyff, ''Nummer 14 Johan Cruyff''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://imdb.com/title/tt0070462|title=Nummer 14 Johan Cruyff|work=IMDb.com|access-date=18 March 2007|archive-date=23 March 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070323071516/http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0070462/|url-status=live}}</ref> and in the Netherlands there is a magazine by [[Voetbal International]], ''Nummer 14''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nummer14.nl|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050205020008/http://nummer14.nl/|url-status=dead|archive-date=5 February 2005|title=Nummer 14|work=Nummer14.com|access-date=18 March 2007}}</ref> He soon benefited from the 4-3-3 formation, which was becoming increasingly standard.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=181}} In November, Cruyff scored six goals against [[AZ Alkmaar]], equaling a record. After winning a replayed KNVB Cup final against [[Sparta Rotterdam]] by a score of 2–1, Ajax won in Europe for the first time. Ajax won the final against [[Panathinaikos Athens]].{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=63}} He signed a seven-year contract at Ajax. At the end of the season, he was named the Dutch and [[European Footballer of the Year]] for 1971.<ref name="FIFA_Profile"/>

[[File:Finale Europacup I in Feijenoord stadion Ajax tegen Inter Milaan 2-0 Johan Cru, Bestanddeelnr 254-9438.jpg|thumb|Cruyff in the final against Inter Milan (31 May 1972)]]
Rinus Michels left Amsterdam after this triumph and moved to Spain, where he took over as manager of FC Barcelona. His successor was the relatively unknown [[Ștefan Kovács]].{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=201}} Kovács had previously managed [[CSA Steaua București (football)|Steaua Bucharest]] in Romania. Unlike Michels, Kovács was not an authoritarian manager; he had a relaxed approach, gave the players much more freedom on and off the pitch, and did not place any value on the strict discipline demanded by Michels. He let his assistant, Bobby Harms, organise training and let the players decide on friendly matches.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=109}} He made only gradual changes. For example, he substituted players less frequently and refrained from varying the team's system and tactics depending on the opponent in European competitions.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=202}} By this time, the mature and well-developed team benefited from this and flourished once again.{{sfn|Wilson|2018|page=11}} Under the new coach, Cruyff assumed an even larger, more dominant role than in Michels' final years and was more than ever a "player-manager" on the pitch. Without the authoritarian Michels, it was Cruyff who demanded discipline verbally and with expressive gestures, argued with the referee, and initiated discussions within the team.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=203}} Under Kovács, the team won the treble of league title, KNVB Cup, and, as the crowning achievement, the European Cup for the second time in a row: In the European Cup final, Inter Milan were defeated 2–0 in a one-sided encounter, with Cruyff scoring both goals. This victory prompted Dutch newspapers to announce the demise of the Italian ''[[catenaccio]]'' style of defensive football in the face of [[Total Football]]. ''Soccer: The Ultimate Encyclopaedia'' says, "Single-handed, Cruyff not only pulled Internazionale of Italy apart in the 1972 European Cup Final, but scored both goals in Ajax's 2–0 win."<ref name="ifhof">{{cite web |title=Johan Cruyff – Hall of Fame |url=http://www.ifhof.com/hof/cruyff.asp |website=International Football Hall of Fame |access-date=2014-05-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190411140420/http://www.ifhof.com/hof/cruyff.asp |archive-date=2019-04-11 |url-status=dead |language=en}}</ref> After declining participation the previous year, Ajax also won the 1972 [[Intercontinental Cup (1960–2004)|Intercontinental Cup]] against Argentina's [[Club Atlético Independiente|Independiente]] in September 1972, followed by the 1972 [[European Super Cup]] in the winter which was won by beating [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]].

In the following season, Kovács' final year, internal tensions within the team increased, and Cruyff, with his status as an outstanding player, provoked jealousies. According to Simon Kuper, the star Cruyff simply had become too big for the Netherlands.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=73}} Under Kovács' again relaxed regime, a lack of fitness became apparent. Instead of offering further spectacular performances, Ajax played with increasing routine and energy conservation; the result was several 1-0 victories. In the end, they won another [[1972–73 Eredivisie|Eredivisie title]]. Internationally, Ajax once again played with [[aplomb]]. On 7 March, the [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]] team built around Franz Beckenbauer and Gerd Müller was thrashed 4–0 in a one-sided match.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=222}} The injured Cruyff did not travel to the return leg in Munich (a 2–1 win for Bayern), which caused irritation among his teammates.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=223}} In the semi-final against Real Madrid, the "Amsterdammers" achieved two comfortable victories to reach the final once again.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=224}} A seasoned Ajax team successfully defended their title in 1973 with a comfortable 1–0 win against [[Juventus FC|Juventus]]. After taking the lead in the 4th minute through [[Johnny Rep]], Ajax avoided any risks and "froze" the game with long passing sequences that prevented the opponent from even getting a touch of the ball.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=224}} Cruyff was awarded the Ballon d'Or as "European Footballer of the Year" in 1973, as he had been in 1971.

===Barcelona and the first La Liga title in 14 years===
{{quote box|width=32%|align=left|quote=When players like [Gareth] [[Gareth Bale|Bale]] and [Cristiano] [[Cristiano Ronaldo|Ronaldo]] are worth around €100 million, Johan [Cruyff] would go in the billions!|source=—[[Franz Beckenbauer]], in an interview with ''[[Bild.de]]'' (September 2014) about Cruyff's transfer value in the early 1970s<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.bild.de/sport/fussball/franz-beckenbauer/cruyff-barcelona-immer-groesser-als-bayern-37721032.bild.html |author=Feindt, Henning |title=Franz Beckenbauer & Johan Cruyff: Der FC Barcelona wird immer größer als der FC Bayern sein |newspaper=[[Bild|Bild.de]] |quote=[[Franz Beckenbauer]]: "Wenn Spieler wie Bale oder Ronaldo um die 100 Millionen wert sind, würde es bei Johan in die Milliarden gehen!" [Original in German] |date=19 September 2014 |access-date=29 September 2016 |archive-date=11 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200811034947/http://www.bild.de/sport/fussball/franz-beckenbauer/cruyff-barcelona-immer-groesser-als-bayern-37721032.bild.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.goal.com/en/news/15/german-football/2014/09/19/5118003/beckenbauer-if-bale-and-ronaldo-are-worth-100m-cruyff-would |author=Tooth, John-Paul |title=Beckenbauer: If Bale and Ronaldo are worth €100m, Cruyff would be worth billions |publisher=Goal.com |date=19 September 2014 |access-date=29 September 2016 |archive-date=3 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200103221414/http://www.goal.com/en/news/15/german-football/2014/09/19/5118003/beckenbauer-if-bale-and-ronaldo-are-worth-100m-cruyff-would |url-status=live }}</ref>}}

Kovács left Ajax in the summer of 1973 and was replaced by coach [[George Knobel]] from [[MVV Maastricht]]. A major incident occurred at the training camp in [[De Lutte]]. [[Piet Keizer]], captain in the 1971–72 season, made it clear that he wanted the captain's armband back, which he had given to Cruyff a year earlier. Keizer argued that Cruyff was too selfish in his business dealings and neglected the well-being of the team.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=227}}

[[File:Johan-cruyff-flying-dutchman-impossible-goal.jpg|thumb|Cruyff played for [[FC Barcelona]] from 1973 to 1978.]]
Cruyff refused and insisted on a vote. New-signing Pim van Dord did not vote, whereupon the remaining 15 players cast their ballots. The vote was 8 to 7 in favour of Keizer. The sulky Cruyff felt humiliated and immediately called his father-in-law, Cor Coster, to whom he expressed his desire to leave, saying: "You must call Barcelona immediately, I want to get out of here." In mid-1973, Cruyff was sold to [[FC Barcelona]] for 6&nbsp;million [[Dutch gulden|guilders]] (approx. US$2&nbsp;million) in a [[World football transfer record|world record transfer fee]]. FC Barcelona had been interested in Cruyff for years; however, offers had been impossible,{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=230}} as foreigners were not eligible to play in the Spanish league from 1962 to 1973.{{sfn|Lowe|2013|page=222}} Furthermore, since Barcelona coach [[Rinus Michels]] viewed Cruyff as a difficult, disruptive character, the management had initially tried to sign [[Gerd Müller]] from Bayern Munich. After a breakdown of negotiations with Müller, Michels agreed to facilitate a transfer for Cruyff. Barcelona's manager Armand Carabén, who was married to a Dutch woman, initiated the negotiations for the transfer. Cruyff, who was still under contract with Ajax, pushed for the transfer by implicitly threatening that he would simply stop playing for Ajax or the national team if the transfer did not go through. As a result, the federation and Ajax initially relented. A last-minute offer from Real Madrid also failed; Cruyff blackmailed the national federation and Ajax with a threat to resign if Ajax sold him to Madrid against his will.{{sfn|Lowe|2013|page=221}} The transfer fee of 6 million guilders made him the most expensive player in the world.{{sfn|Bollen|2021|page=12}}

Cruyff, who was generally apolitical, was unaware of the political situation in Spain at that time. He appreciated Barcelona's climate and the financial opportunities, which far exceeded what he could earn in the Netherlands.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=231}} He defended his move to [[Francoist Spain]], which was criticised in some quarters, with a shrug.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=247}} He was also unaware about the political background of the rivalry between the formerly autonomous [[Catalonia]] on the one hand and [[Castile (historical region)|Castile]], or rather Real Madrid as a symbol of the central government, on the other, and knew nothing about the years of political and cultural discrimination against the regions (especially Catalonia) by the [[Francoist Spain|Franco regime]].{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=252}} When his son was born and the Cruyffs chose the name [[Jordi]] for him, they were unaware that Jordi was the patron saint of Catalonia and that the name had therefore been banned by the Franco government. As part of a general, gradual political liberalisation of the regime in the 1970s, the Cruyffs were allowed to name their son Jordi. This naming was misinterpreted as a political statement and increased Cruyff's popularity.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=251}} It was only in his second year that he began to express some political views, often railing against the (supposed) discrimination against Barça by the central organisation, or Madrid. However, according to his biographers, the entirely apolitical Cruyff always focused on the sporting aspect; he was always referring to the federation and/or the referees, never to Franco's fascist regime itself.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=290}}

In the 1973–74 season, Cruyff cemented his reputation as the best player in the world. Until his registration was completed, Cruyff was ineligible to play in the league, and he and the team instead played some training matches against various, often lower-league, sides, allowing him to gain experience. Cruyff made his competitive debut in front of 90,000 spectators at the Camp Nou on 28 October 1973, against Granada. Cruyff immediately took control as playmaker and scored two goals of his own in a comfortable 4–0 victory. At that time, Barça were only in 14th place in the table, near the relegation zone.{{sfn|Lowe|2013|page=224}} This was followed by a run of four wins, and FC Barcelona took over the top spot in the league. In the next match, their toughest rivals, Atlético Madrid, were beaten 2–1, with Cruyff scoring the opening goal in an acrobatic fashion.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=250}} The goal was featured in the documentary ''{{lang|es|En un momento dado}}'', in which fans of Cruyff attempted to recreate that moment. The goal has been dubbed ''{{lang|es|Le but impossible de Cruyff}}'' ('Cruyff's impossible goal').<ref name="TheGuardian_CruyffRonaldo_2016">{{cite web |title=Johan Cruyff on film, Cristiano Ronaldo is smashing and cricket's thuglife |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/mar/31/johan-cruyff-on-film-cristiano-ronaldo-is-smashing-and-crickets-thuglife |website=The Guardian |date=2016-03-31 |language=en}}</ref>

In mid-February 1974, a demonstration of power followed in the away game against their fiercest rivals [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]] at their home of the [[Santiago Bernabéu Stadium|Santiago Bernabéu]]. In a one-sided match, Cruyff excelled as a goalscorer, provider, and playmaker. Cruyff, who outshone Real's playmaker [[Günter Netzer]], dribbled past three opponents himself and scored the goal to make it 2–0. After that, he sometimes dropped back and was everywhere on the pitch, where he also contributed defensively. The final score was 5–0.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=254}} Thousands of Barcelona fans who watched the match on television poured out of their homes to join in street celebrations.<ref name="Burns">Jimmy Burns (2011). "Barça: A People's Passion". Bloomsbury Publishing,</ref> A ''[[New York Times]]'' journalist wrote that Cruyff had done more for the spirit of the [[Catalonia|Catalan]] people in 90 minutes than many politicians in years of struggle.<ref name="Burns"/> Football historian Jimmy Burns stated, "with Cruyff, the team felt they couldn't lose".<ref name="Burns"/>

The Spanish championship was secured at the beginning of April with a 4–2 victory over [[Sporting de Gijón|Sporting Gijon]]. In Cruyff's debut season, the number of club members (''die socis'') increased from 58,000 the previous year to 64,130.{{sfn|Lowe|2013|page=224}} Until this time, the Madrid derby between Real and Atlético had been the most important match in Spanish football.{{sfn|Lowe|2013|page=178}} Since then, the matches between Real Madrid and FC Barcelona have become the most important fixture in the match calendar; as [[El Clásico]], they remain a cross-sport event into the 21st century.

[[File:FC Barcelona op Schiphol, van links naar rechts Neesken Michels en Cruijff op S, Bestanddeelnr 928-7164.jpg|thumb|Neeskens, Michels and Cruyff (1976)]]
Cruyff's second season in Spain began quite promisingly once again. [[Johan Neeskens]] was signed as a new addition.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=284}} However, Neeskens, known at Barcelona simply as "Johan Segundo", did not provide the hoped-for reinforcement. Since only two foreign players were eligible to play at any one time, the creative and speedy left winger [[Hugo Sotil]] had to make way, which negatively impacted the attacking play. Furthermore, Neeskens struggled to integrate into the team during his first year.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=286}}

The season proved disappointing. At home, Barcelona continued to dominate and play spectacular football.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=286}} In away games, Cruyff was aggressively marked by opposing defenders in an attempt to neutralize him. In his second year, Cruyff missed the preferential treatment he had enjoyed as a star player with referees. He responded by evading man-marking and drifting further into midfield. He also frequently clashed with referees and spectators and received several yellow cards. In February 1975, he was sent off in Malaga after vigorously protesting after a clear offside goal by Malaga. Nevertheless, he refused to leave the pitch and was eventually escorted off by the police.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=288}} Although apolitical, Cruyff quickly seized upon the widespread complaints that the Spanish federation favoured Real Madrid.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=289}} In 1978, Barcelona defeated [[UD Las Palmas|Las Palmas]] 3–1, to win the [[1978 Copa del Rey Final|Copa del Rey]].<ref name="FIFA_Profile"/> Cruyff played two games with [[Paris Saint-Germain F.C.|Paris Saint-Germain]] in 1975 during the Paris tournament. He had only agreed because he was a fan of designer [[Daniel Hechter]], who was then president of PSG.<ref name="SportVintage_CruyffPSG_1975">{{cite web |title=Johan Cruyff au PSG, avec Jean Pierre Dogliani et Just Fontaine (1975) |url=http://www.sport-vintage.com/Library/team%20french/PSG/Johan%20Cruyff%20au%20PSG%20%2C%20avec%20Jean%20Pierre%20Dogliani%20et%20Just%20Fontaine%201975.JPG |website=sport-vintage.com |access-date=2017-04-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716121127/http://www.sport-vintage.com/Library/team%20french/PSG/Johan%20Cruyff%20au%20PSG%20%2C%20avec%20Jean%20Pierre%20Dogliani%20et%20Just%20Fontaine%201975.JPG |archive-date=2011-07-16 |url-status=dead |language=fr}}</ref><ref name="Tumblr_CruyffPhoto_2015">{{cite web |title=Johan Cruyff photograph |url=http://24.media.tumblr.com/tumblr_m68w4idXk21ru2ag8o1_400.jpg |website=Tumblr |access-date=2015-10-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029211119/http://24.media.tumblr.com/tumblr_m68w4idXk21ru2ag8o1_400.jpg |archive-date=2013-10-29 |url-status=dead |language=en}}</ref>

===Brief retirement and spells in the United States===
[[File:Johan Cruijff en voetbalmakelaar Cor Coster (r) op de tribune, Bestanddeelnr 930-4443.jpg|thumb|Cruyff with Cor Coster (on the right), his father-in-law and manager.]]
During the 1976–77 season in Barcelona, the Cruyffs had met French businessman Michel Basilevitch, who was a socis and made a favourable impression on the Cruyffs. Cruyff entrusted him – instead of his father-in-law Cor Coster – with extending his expiring contract with FC Barcelona by one year. Basilevitch was able to negotiate a salary increase, which made the Cruyffs like him all the more. Soon, Basilevitch became a confidant, and he and Cruyff began to establish a company called Grupeco Holding, which invested in various activities, including a pig farm. Critical press reports published that Cruyff had considerable tax debts and that his investments were failures.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=321}}

In 1978, a bank made public that Grupeco Holding could no longer meet its obligations. The investments proved to be almost without exception failures and ended in ruin for Cruyff. His father-in-law got involved and spread in press interviews that Basilevitch had an affair with Cruyff's wife and had enriched himself fraudulently at Cruyff's expense. Basilevitch immediately countered Coster's accusations. He claimed to have suffered losses himself in the bankruptcy of Grupeco Holding and threatened to expose the dubious business practices of Cruyff and Coster, in which he had gained insight as a confidant of the Cruyffs. Coster (and thus also Cruyff) had for years channeled large sums of money past the tax authorities; for example, he claimed hand money for Cruyff was not declared in the tax return, and Coster had in part also transferred funds to Switzerland for the purpose of tax avoidance. Thus Coster was forced to back down. Fearing further revelations about his own business activities, he refrained from further charges.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=327}} Due to the bankruptcy, Cruyff was forced to continue playing as a footballer. He left Spain with enormous debts, which were not even remotely paid off until his return years later.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=330}}

Cruyff and his family moved to the United States.<ref name="SimonKuperFFT">{{cite web |author=Kuper, Simon |author-link=Simon Kuper |date=24 March 2016 |title=Johan Cruyff: The player, the coach, the legacy. [Originally appeared in the July 2009 issue] |url=http://www.fourfourtwo.com/features/johan-cruyff-icon |access-date=18 July 2016 |work=FourFourTwo.com |archive-date=15 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160515214700/http://www.fourfourtwo.com/features/johan-cruyff-icon |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/johan-cruyffs-complicated-legacy/ |author=Schaerlaeckens, Leander |title=Johan Cruyff's Complicated Legacy |publisher=VICE Sports |date=25 March 2016 |access-date=10 July 2020 |archive-date=10 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200610193146/https://www.vice.com/en_au/article/9apbay/johan-cruyffs-complicated-legacy |url-status=live }}</ref> Cruyff insisted that his decision to resume his playing career in the United States was pivotal in his career, stating, "It was wrong, a mistake, to quit playing at 31 with the unique talent I possessed", and adding, "Starting from zero in America, many miles away from my past, was one of the best decisions I made. There I learned how to develop my uncontrolled ambitions, to think as a coach and about sponsorship."<ref name="HeraldScotland">{{cite web |url=http://www.heraldscotland.com/news/12327032.display/ |title=Cruyff the positive thinker looks ahead to new lease of football life |publisher=Herald Scotland (www.heraldscotland.com) |date=26 April 1997 |access-date=26 September 2016 |archive-date=1 October 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161001203133/http://www.heraldscotland.com/news/12327032.display/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In May 1979, Cruyff signed a lucrative deal with the [[Los Angeles Aztecs]] of the [[North American Soccer League (1968–84)|North American Soccer League]] (NASL).<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://newslibrary.naver.com/viewer/index.naver?articleId=1979052300209208013&editNo=2&printCount=1&publishDate=1979-05-23&officeId=00020&pageNo=8&printNo=17730&publishType=00020 |title=축구스타 크루이프 미국프로팀에 입단 |access-date=28 January 2023 |archive-date=28 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230128092500/https://newslibrary.naver.com/viewer/index.naver?articleId=1979052300209208013&editNo=2&printCount=1&publishDate=1979-05-23&officeId=00020&pageNo=8&printNo=17730&publishType=00020 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="FIFA_Profile"/> He had previously been rumoured to be joining the [[New York Cosmos (1971–85)|New York Cosmos]], but the deal did not materialise; he played a few exhibition games for the Cosmos. He stayed at the Aztecs for only one season, and was voted [[NASL Most Valuable Player Award|NASL Player of the Year]]. After considering an offer to join [[Dumbarton F.C.|Dumbarton]] in Scotland, in February 1980, he moved to play for the [[Washington Diplomats]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/time-johan-cruyff-almost-signed-dumbarton-1479973 |title=The time Johan Cruyff almost signed for Dumbarton |work=The Scotsman |date=24 March 2016 |access-date=22 June 2021 |archive-date=18 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518172256/https://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/time-johan-cruyff-almost-signed-dumbarton-1479973 |url-status=live }}</ref> The Cruyffs settled in at Tracy Place, an area with various representative embassies and mansions of politicians, where they formed friendships with diplomats, politicians, and executives. He played the whole 1980 campaign for the Diplomats, even as the team was facing dire financial trouble. At the Diplomats, Cruyff had to fight for his position on the team; he initially clashed with teammates and coach because he skipped team evenings (due to his wife) and smoked in the shower. The team was also accustomed to a completely different style of play than what Cruyff wanted to teach them – the Diplomats played deliberately physical and used to play [[kick and rush]] with long, wide passes, as was done on the British Isles.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=341}}

The frustrated Cruyff soon voiced his complaints about coach and teammates to journalists. However, on the field, he immediately made a difference in class.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=342}} At the Washington Diplomats, he also became familiar with and appreciative of the US-typical sports marketing. He began, at a local TV station, to advertise football. This brought him into contact with [[Eunice Kennedy Shriver]], a member of the [[Kennedy clan]], who had dedicated herself years ago as an activist for the work for people with disabilities and had founded the [[Special Olympics]] in 1968; at her request, Cruyff became an ambassador for the Special Olympics; after this experience, Cruyff began to advocate for disadvantaged children.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=343}} Since the Diplomats had meanwhile declared bankruptcy, Cruyff's time in the USA ended abruptly. Looking back on his years in the US, he later said that this phase had given him back the joy in football that he had temporarily lost.

===Return to Spain with Levante and second spell at Washington Diplomats ===
[[File:Document Cruyff.jpg|thumb|Document issued by [[Levante UD]] to confirm the incorporation of Cruyff to their team]]

Cruyff returned to Europe in November 1980. He became a "technical advisor" at Ajax, where he trained with the team but did not play, and soon fell out and clashed with manager [[Leo Beenhakker]].{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=346}} In January 1981, Cruyff played three friendly matches for [[FC Dordrecht]]. Also in January 1981, manager [[Jock Wallace Jr.|Jock Wallace]] of English club [[Leicester City F.C.|Leicester City]] made an attempt to sign Cruyff, competing with [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] and an unnamed German club for his services,<ref name="Guardian12Jan16">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/in-bed-with-maradona/2016/jan/12/johan-cruyff-signed-leicester-city-barcelona-nasl|title=How Johan Cruyff nearly signed for Leicester City in 1981|newspaper=The Guardian|date=12 January 2016|accessdate=23 December 2021|archive-date=23 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211223021234/https://www.theguardian.com/football/in-bed-with-maradona/2016/jan/12/johan-cruyff-signed-leicester-city-barcelona-nasl|url-status=live}}</ref> and despite negotiations lasting three weeks, in which Cruyff expressed his desire to play for the club, a deal could not be reached.

After the move to English club Leicester City fell through, Cruyff instead chose to sign with Spanish [[Segunda División]] side [[Levante UD|Levante]] in February 1981. His subsequent stint with the Spanish second-division side Levante was also financially rewarding for Cruyff, but entirely unsatisfying from a sporting perspective. His biographer, Auke Kok, considers his time at Levante an absolute low point, both from a professional and a personal standpoint.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=350}} Cruyff, who had not played a match for months, was in poor health and suffering from several minor injuries. Furthermore, he was more preoccupied with the health of his wife Danny, who was initially bedridden after a fall from a horse and, after a deterioration of her condition, had to be admitted to a hospital.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=352}}

On the pitch, Cruyff unsuccessfully attempted to establish his preferred Total Football style of attacking football. The mid-season tactical change proved a complete failure, and Cruyff, plagued by minor injuries, reached his limits in the second division, characterised by its intense physicality. Levante ultimately finished the season in ninth place. Only part of the promised sum was paid to him.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=356}} In May 1981, he then made a highly lucrative guest appearance for AC Milan in a mini-tournament of friendly matches. Due to injury, he only played half a half; before his departure, he promised to make up for it, but this never happened.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=358}} In June 1981, Cruyff returned to the US. He played for the [[Washington Diplomats]] in [[1981 North American Soccer League season|1981 NASL season]].

===Second spell at Ajax===
[[File:Johan Cruijff met Japanse fans.jpg|thumb|Cruyff with Japanese fans in 1982]]

After his spell in the U.S. and his short-lived stay in Spain, Cruyff returned to playing for Ajax in December 1981. Originally, he had rejoined Ajax on 30 November 1980, before his time as a player with Levante, as "technical advisor" to trainer [[Leo Beenhakker]], Ajax being eighth in the league table at the time after 13 games played. After 34 games, Ajax finished the [[1980–81 Eredivisie|1980–81 season]] in second. In December 1981, Cruyff signed a contract as "player" with Ajax until the summer of 1983.<ref name="Murray">Scott Murray, Rowan Walker (2008). "Day of the Match: A History of Football in 365 Days". p. 271. Pan Macmillan, 2008</ref> Alongside an economic crisis in the country, Dutch football had also been in a downward spiral for years.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=361}} Internationally, [[Netherlands national football team|Oranje]] had failed to qualify for the [[1982 FIFA World Cup|1982 finals]]. This decline was accompanied by falling stadium attendances. At his own request, Cruyff signed a performance-based contract with Ajax Amsterdam, which guaranteed him higher earnings if stadium attendance increased. David Winner considers Cruyff's last three seasons, in the autumn of his career, remarkable.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=206}}

As a playmaker, Cruyff inspired a group of young players who formed the backbone of the Oranje's [[1988 European Championship]] title. At 34 years old and no longer at his physical peak, he compensated for his physical shortcomings with his comparatively outstanding understanding of the game and his vision, which allowed him to anticipate game situations earlier than his opponents; a system that Cruyff mastered to perfection during these years, according to his biographers.{{sfn|Schulze-Marmeling|2012|page=106}}{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=93}} He also benefited from a tacit non-aggression pact that opposing coaches made with Cruyff; they instructed their defenders to play "cleanly" and not to foul the crowd-pleaser Cruyff excessively. In addition, Cruyff, as usual, influenced the referees, allowing him to operate largely freely on the pitch. In retrospect, referee Charles Corver later admitted that he had sometimes allowed himself to be manipulated by Cruyff and that his decisions were sometimes influenced by Cruyff.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=382}}

At Ajax, Cruyff encountered a group of talented young players such as [[Frank Rijkaard]], [[Ronald Koeman]], [[Gerald Vanenburg]], and [[Marco van Basten]]; he quickly assumed the leadership role within the team and exerted his influence on both lineup and tactics. In his sold-out home debut against [[HFC Haarlem]], Cruyff dribbled past two opponents in the 22nd minute and scored a goal.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=92}}  With Cruyff, Ajax became significantly more consistent compared to previous years and secured the championship five matchdays before the end of the [[1981–82 Eredivisie|1981–82 season]].{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=366}} In 1982, he scored a famous goal against [[Helmond Sport]]. While playing for Ajax, Cruyff scored a penalty the same way [[Rik Coppens]] had done it 25 years earlier.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2005/oct/26/theknowledge.sport|title=Who took the first two-man penalty?|date=26 October 2005|work=The Guardian|access-date=26 March 2010|location=London, UK|first=James|last=Dart|archive-date=31 October 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131031010620/http://www.theguardian.com/football/2005/oct/26/theknowledge.sport|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://sportscene.excite.co.uk/brazilians-recreate-cruyff-penalty-to-show-pires-and-henry-how-its-done-N2328.html|title=Brazilians recreate Cruyff penalty to show Pires and Henry how it's done|publisher=Excite|date=30 March 2008|access-date=28 October 2013|archive-date=23 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210923184917/http://sportscene.excite.co.uk/brazilians-recreate-cruyff-penalty-to-show-pires-and-henry-how-its-done-N2328.html|url-status=live}}</ref> He put the ball down as for a routine penalty kick, but instead of shooting at goal, Cruyff nudged the ball sideways to teammate [[Jesper Olsen]], who in return passed it back to Cruyff to tap the ball into the empty net, as Otto Versfeld, the Helmond goalkeeper, looked on.{{sfn|Kuper|2022|page=94}} At the end of the [[1982–83 Eredivisie|1982–83]] season, Ajax, along with Cruyff, again became league champions. Additionally Ajax won the [[1982–83 KNVB Cup|Dutch Cup (KNVB-Beker)]].

===Final season at Feyenoord and retirement===
[[File:Feyenoord_tegen_AZ'67_5-2;_Johan_Cruyff_springt_over_doelman_Treytel.jpg|thumb|upright|Feyenoord against AZ'67 5–2; Johan Cruyff jumps over goalkeeper Treytel.]]
After that, Cruyff wanted to extend his contract to play for one last year.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=374}} Ajax board member Tom Harmsen, however, rejected a contract extension.{{sfn|Bollen|2021|page=20}} This angered Cruyff, who responded by signing for Ajax's archrivals [[Feyenoord]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cruyff.com/asp/eng/werkenleven.asp?page=speler-fey|title=Playing for Feyenoord|work=Cruyff.com|access-date=28 October 2013|archive-date=29 October 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029221126/http://cruyff.com/asp/eng/werkenleven.asp?page=speler-fey|url-status=dead}}</ref> Feyenoord's team had been mediocre for years and, apart from the young [[Ruud Gullit]] and [[Peter Houtman]], unlike Ajax, had no highly talented players in its ranks.<ref name="Dutch title">Mik Schots (2013). "Feyenoord-Ajax: gezworen vijanden". Singel Uitgeverijen</ref> On the seventh matchday, Feyenoord faced Ajax in "[[De Klassieker]]" in Amsterdam; the game was lost 8–2. A defiant Cruyff nevertheless declared after the game: "We will win the championship."{{sfn|Bollen|2021|page=50}} Feyenoord also suffered heavy defeats in the European Cup; in the game against Tottenham Hotspur, Cruyff was completely neutralised by his opponent [[Glenn Hoddle]].{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=378}}

Undeterred by these initial defeats, Cruyff influenced tactics, training, and lineup, importing his football knowledge. While rival Ajax played erratically, Cruyff's well-organised Feyenoord usually won unspectacularly but consistently and was already leading the table by winter. In February 1984, Ajax were first defeated in the KNVB Cup, then 4–1 in the second leg of the league season, with Cruyff also scoring a goal.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=381}} At the end of the season, the team won the double of [[1983–84 Eredivisie|league title]] and [[1983–84 KNVB Cup|KNVB Cup]]. Because of his performance on the field, he was voted as Dutch Footballer of the Year for the fifth time. On 13 May 1984, he played his last match against Zwolle. He rejected offers from the club to extend his contract, as he was no longer able to meet the physical demands of the game.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=383}}  Cruyff played his last game in Saudi Arabia against [[Al-Ahli SC (Jeddah)|Al-Ahli]], bringing Feyenoord back into the game with a goal and an assist.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://fm.manutd.nl/de-echte-afscheidswedstrijd-van-cruijff|title=De echte afscheidswedstrijd van Cruijff|publisher=Football United|date=20 July 2009|language=nl|access-date=28 October 2013|archive-date=20 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160420175652/http://fm.manutd.nl/de-echte-afscheidswedstrijd-van-cruijff/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==International career==
[[File:Cruyff1974.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Cruyff as captain of the Netherlands prior to a game at the 1974 World Cup]]

As a Dutch international, Cruyff played 48 [[Cap (sport)|matches]], scoring 33 goals.<ref name="FIFA_Profile"/><ref>{{cite news|title=The total footballer|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sportacademy/hi/sa/football/features/newsid_3301000/3301407.stm|publisher=BBC|access-date=19 July 2014|archive-date=24 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211224184724/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sportacademy/hi/sa/football/features/newsid_3301000/3301407.stm|url-status=live}}</ref> The national team never lost a match in which Cruyff scored. On 7 September 1966, he made his official debut for the Netherlands in the [[UEFA Euro 1968]] [[UEFA Euro 1968 qualifying|qualifier]] against [[Hungary national football team|Hungary]], scoring in the 2–2 draw. In his second match, a friendly against [[Czechoslovakia national football team|Czechoslovakia]], Cruyff was the first Dutch international to receive a [[Misconduct (football)|red card]]. The [[Royal Dutch Football Association]] (KNVB) banned him from international games, but not the Eredivisie or KNVB Cup.{{sfn|Winner|2008}}

Accusations of Cruyff's "aloofness" were not rebuffed by his habit of wearing a shirt with only two black stripes along the sleeves, as opposed to [[Adidas]]' usual design feature of three, worn by all the other Dutch players. Cruyff also had a separate sponsorship deal with [[Puma SE|Puma]].<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2001/may/30/theknowledge.sport | location=London | work=The Guardian | first1=Scott | last1=Murray | first2=Sean | last2=Ingle | title=A tale of strips, stripes and strops | date=30 May 2001 | access-date=11 December 2016 | archive-date=29 April 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160429065853/http://www.theguardian.com/football/2001/may/30/theknowledge.sport | url-status=live }}</ref> From 1970 onwards, he wore the number 14 jersey for the Netherlands, setting a trend for wearing shirt numbers outside the usual starting line-up numbers of 1 to 11.<ref name="FIFA_Profile"/>

=== World Cup 1974 ===
Before training camp, Cruyff initiated tough negotiations with the federation regarding bonuses and lucrative sponsorship deals. During the training camp, Cruyff and the Ajax players quickly reconciled. Neither side had any interest in reviving old disputes and they quickly came to an understanding. At the training camp in [[Zeist]], Cruyff and the Ajax group were the dominant force. Rinus Michels, appointed as coach, constantly commuted between the Netherlands and Spain, where he was coaching FC Barcelona in the cup competition. Therefore, Cruyff played a key role; he assumed the role of player-coach (now with Michels' blessing) and dictated tactics as well as parts of the starting lineup. Players whom Cruyff criticised or who did not acknowledge the dominance of the "Amsterdammers" were immediately sidelined or sent home.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=263}}

The experienced first-choice goalkeeper, [[Jan van Beveren]], defied the "Amsterdammers" and was promptly sent home. Instead, at Cruyff's instigation, [[Jan Jongbloed]] was installed as the first-choice goalkeeper. Cruyff justified this not only as part of the group dynamics within the team, but also saw Jongbloed as the better player with the ball and a disguised libero, which in his eyes was important due to the team's attacking style. The [[Libero (association football)|libero]] role was also determined by Cruyff, who assigned the task to midfielder [[Arie Haan]]; while he had had disagreements with Haan at Ajax in 1973, he nevertheless valued his passing accuracy. In addition, [[Wim Rijsbergen]] from Feyenoord Rotterdam was installed as the second central defender. Tactically, according to Cruyff's vision, Oranje were to play a riskier version of Total Football, as practiced by Ajax.{{sfn|Kok|2022|page=263}}

[[File:WK 74 Nederlands elftal traint in Hiltrup, spelers delen handtekingen uit, Bestanddeelnr 927-2561.jpg|thumb|A relaxed Cruyff is giving autographs at Hiltrup]]
In their opening match in Hanover, the Netherlands defeated a defensively minded [[Uruguay national football team|Uruguay]] 2–0. In the second game against [[Sweden men's national football team|Sweden]], Cruyff performed the so-called "Cruyff Turn";{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=130}}<ref name="YouTube_CruyffTurn_2006">{{cite av media |title=Johan Cruyff turn |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U1k7DGqRF5g |via=[[YouTube]] |publisher=Roeboe |date=2006-03-02 |language=en}}</ref> he kicked the ball so suddenly with his heel past his own leg that the startled defender Jan Olsson lost his footing. Cruyff had been using this move for years in the Netherlands, so it no longer attracted much attention from Dutch reporters and the public, but for the rest of the football world, it was a defining moment of the World Cup. In their 4–1 victory in the third group match against Bulgaria, the Netherlands thrilled the crowd. Cruyff was clearly the star, directing the team, creating gaps with his pacey dribbling and delivering precise long passes.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=131}}

In the second group stage, the Dutch national team, led by Cruyff, improved once again and reached the peak of their abilities. In the opening match of the second group stage against [[Argentina national football team|Argentina]], Cruyff again dominated the game; with his first touch, he rounded the Argentine goalkeeper Carnevali in the eleventh minute and scored to make it 1–0. After that, the team conserved their energy for a long time, with Cruyff remaining passive and only playing passes from a stationary position. In the 72nd minute, he set up the third goal and then scored the fourth goal himself.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=132}}

Against [[East Germany national football team|East Germany]], they achieved an easy victory. Cruyff initiated both of the Netherlands' goals as the provider. The final group match against [[Brazil national football team|Brazil]] was like a semi-final. Both sides played a very physical game from the start, resulting in many hard fouls. After just a few minutes, Cruyff was denied by the goalkeeper from close range. The first half was evenly matched, and the Netherlands were fortunate when Brazil players [[Valdomiro (footballer, born 1946)|Valdomiro]] and [[Jairzinho]] both missed two clear chances. Cruyff decided the game with two actions after the break. First, he played a one-two with Neeskens, who scored to make it 1–0. A quarter of an hour later, he converted a cross from [[Ruud Krol]] to make it 2–0. After that, the game descended into chaos; there were several frustrated fouls by the beaten Brazilians, and [[Luís Pereira]] received a red card. The Netherlands advanced to the final, where they were considered as clear favourites over the hosts [[Germany national football team|West Germany]]. The football world was thrilled by the seemingly effortless play of these victories and raved about the team's artistry. While the other teams, due to the changed security situation after the 1972 Munich Olympics attack, kept a tight rein on themselves, the self-assured Netherlands maintained a much more open approach at their headquarters in Hiltrup; Cruyff himself gave interviews and signed autographs there almost on a daily basis.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=132}}

Before the final, a scandal erupted over the infamous pool party: Cruyff and some other players had partied with girls the day before the match against Brazil, and the German [[Bild newspaper]] published a story the next day with the headline: ''Cruyff, Champagne, Naked Girls and a Cool Bath''. In the days that followed, Cruyff had to repeatedly justify himself to his wife in hours-long phone calls, as she called repeatedly and threatened divorce. The sleep-deprived Cruyff, fearing for his marriage, was less concerned with the opponent than with the pool party story.<ref>Dietrich Schulze-Marmeling, Hubert Dahlkamp: ''Die Geschichte der Fußball-Weltmeisterschaft 1930–2006.'' Verlag Die Werkstatt, Göttingen 2006, p. 238.</ref>

[[File:Bundesarchiv Bild 183-N0716-0314, Fußball-WM, BRD - Niederlande 2-1.jpg|thumb|Cruyff in the final, pursued by [[Berti Vogts]], shortly before he is fouled by [[Uli Hoeneß|Hoeneß]]]]
In the Netherlands, the events surrounding the pool party were considered crucial; however, it was ignored for years that the Netherlands had not prepared at all for the game against the West German team, as coach Michels was in Barcelona in the days before the final and the assistant coach responsible for observing the opponents had been sent home early. In the final in Munich, after the kickoff and some initial ball circulation among the Elftal players, Cruyff received the ball at the centre circle within seconds, hesitated briefly, and then suddenly surged towards goal, followed by his marker, [[Berti Vogts]]. Cruyff was fouled by [[Uli Hoeneß]] on the edge of the penalty area; referee [[Jack Taylor (referee)|Jack Taylor]] immediately awarded a penalty, which Neeskens converted.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=136}} The Germans had not yet touched the ball. After the goal, the German team was visibly shaken, but the Dutch national team did not press forward. Instead, they confidently circulated the ball amongst themselves without looking for a shot, and the German team recovered.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=137}}

The German team gained the initiative and was able to equalise through a penalty won by [[Bernd Hölzenbein]]. The German team began to dominate the game at times. Cruyff's influence was stifled by the effective marking of Vogts. Cruyff dropped deep into midfield, and disappeared completely for long periods of the game.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=138}} A goal by [[Gerd Müller]] gave West Germany a 2–1 lead at halftime. At halftime, the protesting Cruyff had a verbal altercation with the referee and received a yellow card. After the break, the Netherlands launched a furious attack, but the score remained unchanged, and Oranje ultimately lost to the host nation. The German sports journalist Ulfert Schröder called Munich "the melancholic high point" of Cruyff's career.{{sfn|Schulze-Marmeling|2012|page=169}} While [[Franz Beckenbauer]] said of Cruyff that "Johan was the better player, but I am a world champion", Cruyff, who was voted the [[Golden Ball (FIFA)|tournament's best player]], repeatedly described the defeat in later years as a moral victory. The lost final, however, became a Dutch trauma.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=125}}

===Euro 1976===
Between 1974 and 1976, the Netherlands played successfully in the qualifying rounds for the [[UEFA Euro 1976|1976 European Championship]], in which four teams participated.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=263}} Michels had been replaced by George Knobel, who submitted unconditionally to Cruyff and gave him free rein. In response to Cruyff's dominance, PSV players Jan van Beveren and Willy van der Kuylen retired from the national team. Before Euro 1976, Cruyff again initiated negotiations with the federation regarding bonuses and sponsorship contracts, which dragged on and on and completely overshadowed the sporting aspect. The federation and the Cruyff/Knobel duo were also at odds over the Chef d'équipe.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=264}} The match against Czechoslovakia was actually intended by the self-confident Dutch as merely a warm-up before a rematch against Germany,{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=263}} but turned out to be completely different. The Czechs disrupted the Dutch rhythm and took an early lead.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=267}} In the end, it was a clear defeat.{{sfn|Winner|2008|page=268}} Cruyff left before the third-place match to undergo knee surgery in Barcelona.

===After 1976===
Cruyff retired from international football in October 1977, having helped the national team qualify for the upcoming World Cup.<ref name="FIFA_Profile"/> Without him, the Netherlands finished runners-up in the World Cup again. Initially, there were two rumours as to his reason for missing the [[1978 FIFA World Cup|1978 World Cup]]: either he missed it for political reasons ([[National Reorganization Process|a military dictatorship was in power]] in Argentina at that time), or that his wife dissuaded him from playing.<ref>{{Cite web|url = https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/apr/17/newsstory.sport|title = After 30 years, the truth behind Cruyff's World Cup absence|website = [[TheGuardian.com]]|date = 16 April 2008|access-date = 23 August 2016|archive-date = 21 September 2022|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20220921091415/https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/apr/17/newsstory.sport|url-status = live}}</ref> In 2008, Cruyff stated to the journalist [[Antoni Bassas]] in [[Catalunya Ràdio]] that he and his family were subject to a kidnap attempt in Barcelona a year before the tournament, and that this had caused his retirement. "To play a World Cup you have to be 200% okay, there are moments when there are other values in life."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/apr/16/newsstory.sport15|work=The Guardian|title=Kidnappers made Cruyff miss World Cup|date=16 April 2008|access-date=26 March 2010|location=London, UK|first=Paul|last=Doyle|archive-date=20 April 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080420073157/http://football.guardian.co.uk/News_Story/0,,2273925,00.html?|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Coaching career==
===Entry into management with Ajax===
{{multiple image
|align = right
|direction = horizontal
|total_width = 400
|image1 = Vertrek Ajax van Schiphol voor Europa Cup II wedstrijd tegen Olympiakos Piraeus, Bestanddeelnr 933-8034.jpg 
|image2 = Training Ajax, Cruijff (r) en algemeen directeur Arie van Eijden tijdens perscon, Bestanddeelnr 934-1215.jpg
|footer = Two images of Cruyff as Ajax manager: (left): with [[Marco van Basten|Van Basten]] and [[Frank Rijkaard|Rijkaard]] in 1986; (right): during a press conference in November 1987
}}
After retiring from playing, Cruyff followed in the footsteps of his mentor [[Rinus Michels]]. In June 1985, Cruyff returned to Ajax again. He coached a young Ajax side to victory in the [[UEFA Cup Winners' Cup|European Cup Winners' Cup]] in [[1987 European Cup Winners' Cup Final|1987]] (1–0). In the [[1985–86 Eredivisie|1985–86 season]], the league title was lost to [[Jan Reker]]'s PSV, despite Ajax having a goal difference of +85 (120 goals for, 35 goals against). In the 1985–86 and [[1986–87 Eredivisie|1986–87]] seasons, Ajax won the KNVB Cup.

It was during this period as manager that Cruyff was able to implement his favoured team formation—three mobile [[Defender (association football)|defenders]]; plus one more covering space – becoming, in effect, a [[Midfielder|defensive midfielder]] (from [[Frank Rijkaard|Rijkaard]], [[Danny Blind|Blind]], [[Sonny Silooy|Silooy]], [[Frank Verlaat|Verlaat]], [[Peter Larsson (footballer, born 1961)|Larsson]], [[Ronald Spelbos|Spelbos]]), two "controlling" midfielders (from Rijkaard, [[Arnold Scholten|Scholten]], [[Aron Winter|Winter]], [[Jan Wouters|Wouters]], [[Arnold Mühren|Mühren]], [[Rob Witschge|Witschge]]) with responsibilities to feed the attack-minded players, one [[Forward (association football)|second striker]] ([[John Bosman|Bosman]], Scholten), two touchline-hugging [[Winger (football)|wingers]] (from [[Dennis Bergkamp|Bergkamp]], [[John van't Schip|van't Schip]], [[Rob de Wit (footballer)|De Wit]], [[Richard Witschge|Witschge]]) and one versatile centre forward (from [[Marco van Basten|Van Basten]], [[Henny Meijer|Meijer]], Bosman).

===Return to Barcelona as manager and building "the Dream Team"===
After having appeared for the club as a player, Cruyff returned to Barcelona for the [[1988–89 FC Barcelona season|1988–89 season]], this time to take up his new role as coach of the first team. In 1988, FC Barcelona was going through major turbulence both on and off the field. Since Cruyff's departure in 1978, there had been a lack of an overarching sporting philosophy, and the playing style had varied with each coach in charge. English coach [[Terry Venables]] had guided Barça to their first championship title since 1974 in 1985. In 1986, the team reached the final of the European Cup (in [[Seville]]) but lost in a penalty shootout to the clear underdog [[CSA Steaua București (football)|Steaua Bucharest]], which went down in the club's and fans' history as the "Seville trauma". The defeat undermined Venables' position at the club and subjected him to ongoing criticism; among other things, Venables was accused of favouring the British players. After an unsuccessful following season, he was dismissed and replaced by [[Luis Aragonés]]. Under Aragonés, the team again played a disappointing season and were eliminated in the UEFA Cup quarter-finals by [[Bayer 04 Leverkusen|Bayer Leverkusen]]. In the championship, by April 1988, the team was already 23 points behind the eventual champions Real Madrid. At this moment, the 'Hesperia mutiny'<ref>President Núñez had reduced the players' salaries. Salaries were cut in half, but separate contracts were drawn up to buy the players' image rights. This model was extremely lucrative for both club and the players, as the image rights contracts were taxed at a significantly lower rate. After tax inspectors discovered this, Núñez blamed the players.
